0.title: What Matters Most
0.essay:
Ask most Christians what matters most to God, and they will give the right answer: love. Love God, and love your neighbour. But ask what that means on a Tuesday morning, with a full inbox and a sharp-tongued relative, and the answer often goes vague. Is love a feeling? A decision? A duty? This study answers plainly.

The question put to Jesus

In the last week of his life, a lawyer asked Jesus, “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” (Matthew 22:36). Jesus answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37–40).

Jesus did not invent these words. The first comes from the creed every Israelite knew by heart, the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). The second comes from a chapter of practical laws: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus set them side by side, and the whole Bible hangs on them.

Is love a feeling?

Many of us assume that love is a feeling, and that if I do not feel it, I do not have it. Others think love is simply duty. Scripture will not let us settle in either place. In brief: love for God is not first a feeling, and it is not mere duty. It is the whole person turned toward God: treasuring him, trusting him, delighting in him and obeying him. Feelings belong to it, but they rise and fall like the tide and are not its measure. Love for our neighbour is the same turning, directed outward: a settled will to seek another person’s good, for God’s sake and at cost to ourselves, whether or not we feel warm toward them. And all of it begins not with our love but with his.

Where we are going

We start with God’s love for us, because that is where the Bible starts, and end with what to do when love grows cold. The study The Ten Commandments shows how the law spells out these two commands in detail; this study looks at the love itself. The Fear of the Lord shows how fear and love belong together.

The chapters

He Loved Us First; What Love Is; Heart, Soul, Mind and Strength; Do You Love Me?; Your Neighbour as Yourself; and When Love Grows Cold.

For reflection

If someone asked you what it means to love God, what would you say? Do you tend to think of love mainly as a feeling or mainly as a duty?

1.title: He Loved Us First
1.essay:
Before you read another word about how to love God, read this: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). Christian love never starts with us. It is an answer.

A command we cannot keep

All your heart, all your soul, all your mind, all your strength. All, always, and every neighbour cared for as readily as yourself. Who has done this for a single hour?

The great commandment reaches past what we do to what we prize. A person can avoid murder and adultery and still love money, comfort or reputation more than God. When a lawyer recited the two commands, Jesus replied, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live” (Luke 10:28). The lawyer’s next move tells us everything: “But he, desiring to justify himself” (Luke 10:29), asked a question to narrow the command down. That is what we all do with the law of love. We shrink it until we can manage it.

Honestly faced, the great commandment shows us how little love we have. At the root of every sin is a failure of love: we have loved created things more than the Creator, and ourselves more than our neighbour.

One man kept it

There has been one exception. Jesus Christ loved his Father with all his heart, soul, mind and strength, every moment of his life. “I always do the things that are pleasing to him,” he said (John 8:29). And he loved his neighbour not only as himself but more than himself. He touched lepers, ate with outcasts, and gave his life for people who had abandoned him. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1).

The great commandment, fully kept, looks like Jesus. And here is the gospel: he kept it in our place. His perfect love for God and neighbour is counted to everyone who trusts him, and his death bore the judgment our lovelessness deserved. So the first word to a believer about the great commandment is not “Try harder”, but the word Jesus spoke from the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Loved while still enemies

Notice when God’s love came to us. Not when we were improving. “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). God did not wait to be loved before he loved. He loved people who had no love for him at all, and his love made them lovers.

This is unlike our love. We love what is already lovely. God’s love is not drawn out by our beauty. It creates beauty where there was none. Moses told Israel that God did not set his love on them because they were many, “but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:8). The reason for God’s love is found in God.

We love because he first loved us

John draws the conclusion in six words: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Our love for God is a response, never an achievement. It is like the warmth in a stone that has lain in the sun: real warmth, but every bit of it received.

If love for God were an achievement, the great commandment would leave us anxious, always checking the temperature of our hearts. Because it is a response, the way to love God more is not to stare at our love but to look at his. Love is kindled by being loved. The more clearly we see what God has done in Christ, the more our cold hearts begin to warm.

It is God himself, too, who gives the new heart that can respond. Moses commanded Israel to love God, and then promised: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 30:6). What the law demanded, God promised to give. In the new covenant he keeps that promise by his Spirit: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

An example

A man in his fifties has been a church member for decades. He is reliable and respected, and privately has always felt that God is a little disappointed in him. One evening, preparing for his home group, he stops at 1 John 4:10 and reads it three times. It dawns on him that he has spent his life trying to love God enough to be loved back. He simply thanks God, slowly, for loving him first. Something in him that has been clenched for years begins to loosen.

The wonder of it

Pause over what this means. The God who needs nothing, who has known perfect love for ever as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, chose to love rebels, and paid for that love with the blood of his Son. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). Everything else in this study grows from that root.

For reflection

Have you tended to think of loving God as something you must achieve? How does 1 John 4:10 change that? Where have you shrunk the great commandment to something you can manage? What does it mean to you that Christ kept the law of love in your place?

2.title: What Love Is
2.essay:
So what is love for God? Not first a feeling, and not mere duty. It is the whole person turned toward God in delight, trust and obedience. Getting this right spares us much needless guilt, and some false comfort.

Not first a feeling

Feelings matter in the Bible. The psalmists do not love God coolly. “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God” (Psalm 42:1).

But feelings are not the foundation, and they are not the measure. Emotions are shaped by sleep, illness, grief and a hundred other things. The same psalm that pants for God also asks, “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?” (Psalm 42:5). The psalmist’s feelings were low, yet his love was holding on: he was still speaking to God and still hoping in him. If love were only a feeling, it would vanish every time we were tired, and no one could obey the command on demand.

Not mere duty

Yet love is not mere duty either. You can keep rules for God without loving him at all. Paul says a person could give away everything and even die a martyr’s death, “but have not love” (1 Corinthians 13:3). Duty without love turns bitter, like the elder brother in Jesus’ parable, who served his father for years and never enjoyed him (Luke 15:29–30).

The whole self turned toward God

To love God is to value him above all things, to want him, to delight in him, to trust him, and to give ourselves to him in obedience. It is a turning of the whole person, mind, will, desires and actions, toward God as our greatest good.

Older Christian writers made a helpful distinction between affections and passions. Passions are surges of emotion that come and go. Affections are the settled inclinations of the heart: what we prize, what we lean toward, what we would choose if everything else were taken away. Love for God is an affection in this sense. It usually brings feelings with it, but it can be present and real when the feelings are quiet. A mother up all night with a sick child may feel only exhaustion, yet no one doubts that she loves.

Love and obedience

Jesus ties love and obedience closely together. “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me” (John 14:21). John says, “For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3).

Jesus does not say obedience is love, as if love were nothing but rule-keeping. He says love will keep his commandments. Obedience is the shape love takes, the way it shows itself. Love obeys, and obedience is sweetened by love. That is why John can say the commandments are not burdensome. They are the wishes of someone we love.

Love as delight

At its heart, love for God is delight in God himself, not only in his gifts. “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:25–26). The old catechisms said that our chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever, and those two belong together. God is honoured when he is enjoyed.

Rightly ordered loves

Augustine taught that sin is not so much a lack of love as love in the wrong order. We were made to love God first and most, and everything else in him and for his sake. Sin turns that order upside down. We love good things more than the God who gave them. These displaced loves are idols. “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

The answer is not to love created things coldly, but to love God more. A man who loves Christ more than his wife will love her better, not worse, because he no longer needs her to be his god. When Jesus said, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37), he was not calling for cold families but for rightly ordered hearts.

When feelings come and go

So what about the days when you feel nothing? First, do not conclude that love has died. Ask instead: do I still want God, still turn to him, however feebly? Would I give him up if I could? Peter, after denying Jesus, could still say, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). His feelings were probably a tangle of shame and grief. But the direction of his heart was clear.

Second, keep doing what love does. Pray, read, gather with God’s people, obey in the next small thing. Feelings often follow actions. When they return, receive them as gifts, without making them the test of everything.

An example

A young mother with two children under three tells her pastor she thinks she no longer loves God. She used to weep in worship; now she can barely stay awake through a sermon. He asks a few questions. She still prays, in snatches. She wants God very much. She clings to him. He tells her gently that what she has lost is mostly sleep, not love. Her love is being expressed in a hundred hidden acts of care done for God’s sake, and in a stubborn clinging that does not depend on feelings.

For reflection

Have you ever judged your love for God by your feelings alone? What happened? How does Jesus connect love and obedience in John 14? Which of your loves most often climbs above God, and what would it look like to put it back in its place? Read Psalm 73:25–26 slowly. Can you pray it, even weakly?

3.title: Heart, Soul, Mind and Strength
3.essay:
Jesus did not only say “love God”. He said with all your heart, all your soul, all your mind and all your strength. Each word opens a door into ordinary life. But first notice the word that is repeated four times: all.

Wholeheartedness

The four words are not four compartments,. They overlap, and the Gospels themselves vary them. Deuteronomy has heart, soul and might. Matthew has heart, soul and mind. Mark and Luke have all four, in different orders (Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27). The point is that no part of us is left out. God does not want a share of us. He wants us.

That is what was said of Josiah, the reforming king: he “turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might” (2 Kings 23:25). And it is the opposite of what the psalmist found in himself when he prayed, “unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11). By nature our hearts are divided, and only God can unite them.

With all your heart

In the Bible the heart is not mainly the seat of the emotions, as it is in our way of speaking. It is the control centre of the person, where we think, desire, choose and decide. “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). To love God with all your heart means that your deepest desires and your will are set on him.

What do you reach for when you are anxious? What would you most hate to lose? Jesus said, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). The heart follows the treasure. Loving God with all your heart means that he is the treasure, and that you keep choosing him when other treasures call.

With all your soul

The Hebrew word translated “soul” (nephesh) does not mean a ghostly part of us that floats free of the body. It means the living self, the whole life of a person. To love God with all your soul is to love him with your whole life, and if need be with your life itself.

For most of us it means something quieter. God is not one department of life, kept for Sundays, but the one to whom all of life belongs: work and rest, family and friendships, hobbies and holidays. Paul puts it simply: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

With all your mind

Loving God involves thinking. The Gospels add “mind” to make plain what the Hebrew word for heart already included. To love him with your mind is to want to know him truly: to read his word carefully, to think about what it means, to ask questions, to learn, and to let your opinions be corrected by Scripture. “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2).

It also means bringing our thinking under his rule in the rest of life. A Christian accountant, scientist, nurse or plumber loves God with the mind by doing careful, honest, intelligent work, and by guarding what we feed our minds on. Yet knowledge alone is not love. “This ‘knowledge’ puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The mind that loves God learns in order to worship and serve, not to win arguments.

With all your strength

The word in Deuteronomy translated “might” is unusual. It normally means “very” or “exceedingly”, so the command is almost: love God with all your “muchness”, everything you have. Some ancient Jewish teachers took it to include a person’s possessions. Strength means body, energy, time, abilities and money: all the resources we have to spend.

So loving God with all your strength is very practical. It is the hours you give, the effort you put into your work “as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), the money you give away, the care you take of a body that is “a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19). It is also accepting your limits. Strength varies. God asks for all of what you have, not for what someone else has.

Not a checklist

This is not a fourfold audit to condemn us. No one but Christ has loved God this way, and he did it for us. The four words show how wide love’s territory is, and how wide his love for us was. He gave his whole self for us: heart, soul, mind and body, nailed to a cross. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Wholehearted love answers wholehearted love.

An example

A retired engineer decides to read through the Gospels slowly with a notebook, something he has never done in forty years of churchgoing. Over a year his giving grows and he starts visiting a housebound neighbour. Nothing is dramatic, but his faith, which had been a Sunday matter, has spread into his mind, his time, his hands and his money. It feels less like new duties than like coming home.

For reflection

Which of the four, heart, soul, mind or strength, do you find hardest to give to God? Where in your week is God treated as one department among many? What is one way you could love God with your mind this month? How does Christ’s wholehearted love for you make the command less crushing and more inviting?

4.title: Do You Love Me?
4.essay:
The New Testament keeps the command to love God, and gives it a face. Peter writes to people who had never seen him: “Though you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8). Christian love for God is love for God made known in his Son.

Why love centres on Jesus

This is not a move away from loving God. Jesus is God the Son, made flesh. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). That is why the New Testament makes love for Christ a mark of a true Christian. Paul ends Ephesians, “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible” (Ephesians 6:24). He ends 1 Corinthians with a sober warning: “If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed” (1 Corinthians 16:22).

Jesus himself puts love for him at the centre. “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23). Love for Christ is not a religious mood; it is the doorway into fellowship with the triune God.

By a charcoal fire

Peter had once boasted that even if all the others fell away, he never would (Matthew 26:33). Then, warming himself at a charcoal fire, he denied Jesus three times. After the resurrection, by another charcoal fire on the shore of Galilee, Jesus asked him three times, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:16). The first time he added, “more than these?” (John 21:15). Peter made no comparisons now. In the end he simply said, “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17).

Jesus was restoring Peter, letting each denial be answered by a confession of love. And with each answer came a task: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep. Love for Christ shows itself in caring for the people Christ loves. And Peter rested his claim not on his record or his feelings but on Jesus’ knowledge of him. A Christian whose love is weak can still rest there.

Forgiven much, loving much

Luke tells of a dinner at the house of a Pharisee named Simon. A woman known in the town as a sinner came in, wept over Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair, kissed them and anointed them. Jesus told him a story about two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, both forgiven. “Now which of them will love him more?” (Luke 7:42). Then Jesus said of the woman, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little” (Luke 7:47).

Her love did not earn her forgiveness. The story makes plain that the forgiveness came first and the love flowed from it; at the end Jesus tells her, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). Her love was the evidence of how much she knew she had been forgiven. Simon thought he had little to be forgiven, and so he loved little. The person who thinks he is basically decent will find it hard to love Jesus warmly. The person who has seen the size of her debt, and the size of his mercy, cannot help it.

So if your love for Christ feels thin, one place to look is your sense of sin. Not to wallow in it, but to see it truly, so that you see grace truly. “For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14).

How love for Christ grows

We cannot make ourselves love Christ by straining to feel it. But we can put ourselves where love grows. Love grows by seeing. “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Behold him in his word. Read the Gospels to look at Jesus. You cannot love someone you do not know.

Meet him at his table. In the Lord’s Supper, Christ sets before us the signs of his body given and his blood shed. This commentary holds, with the Reformed tradition, that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and that believers feed on him by faith. Come to it hungry, not proud of your love but needing his.

Speak to him in prayer. Love grows in conversation. Prayer is not only asking; it is time spent with someone you love.

Follow him in obedience. “And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). Those who obey Jesus come to know him more. Obedience is not only the fruit of love but one of the ways love is fed.

An example

A woman in her forties came to faith after years of heavy drinking and of hurting people she loved. A quiet older man at her church, puzzled by how eagerly she talks about Jesus, admits to her one day that he envies her. He has never felt he needed much forgiving. Over the following months, as he reads Luke 7 and honestly examines his pride, his coldness and his quiet judgments of others, he finds to his surprise that he too has been forgiven much. His love for Christ, long correct, begins to be warm.

For reflection

If Jesus asked you whether you love him, what would you say, and on what would you rest your answer? Why does the woman in Luke 7 love so much? Do you see yourself more like her or like Simon? Which of the four ways of growing in love for Christ do you most neglect? Read a Gospel story this week simply to look at Jesus.

5.title: Your Neighbour as Yourself
5.essay:
Jesus said the second commandment is like the first. The two cannot be pulled apart. “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4:20). Love for God that does not spill over into love for people is not the real thing.

Who is my neighbour?

The lawyer who wanted to justify himself asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). He wanted a boundary. Jesus answered with the story of the good Samaritan. A priest and a Levite pass by a beaten man; a Samaritan, one of a despised people, stops, binds his wounds and pays for his care.

Then Jesus turned the question round. “Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” (Luke 10:36). The lawyer had asked, in effect, Whom must I love? Jesus asks, Will you be a neighbour? Your neighbour is anyone God puts in your path whose need you are able to meet. No one is outside the circle, whatever their race, religion, politics or reputation. Already in Leviticus, God said of the stranger living among his people, “you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34).

What does “as yourself” mean?

Some today read “love your neighbour as yourself” as two commands: first learn to love yourself, and then you will be able to love others. Others read it as an assumption: we already love ourselves, and that natural care is the measure of our care for others. The first view often has real hurts in mind.

This commentary’s view: “as yourself” is a measure, not a second command. Scripture never tells us to love ourselves; it assumes that we do. “For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29). Augustine and Calvin both observed that no command was needed for us to love ourselves. Jesus’ golden rule says the same: “So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12). Turn the energy you spend on your own needs outward. The answer to self-hatred is not a programme of self-love but the love of God, who knows the worst about us and loves us still. The studies Shame and Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation take that further.

What love does

Love for a neighbour, like love for God, is not first a feeling. It is a settled will to seek another person’s good, and it shows itself in action. Paul’s description is made almost entirely of verbs: “Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5). There is hardly a feeling in the list.

John makes it concrete. “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:16–18). Love is measured at the cross and practised with money, meals and time. So love is “the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10).

When you do not feel it

You do not have to like someone in order to love them. You may never feel warm toward a prickly colleague, but you can still be patient, speak well of them, pray for them and do them good. C. S. Lewis observed that when we behave as if we loved someone, we often come to love them. But even if warmth never comes, the love is real, and God sees it.

Love, truth and limits

Love is not the same as being nice. Love “does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). Sometimes love says hard things, “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Sometimes it says no. Leviticus 19, the very chapter that commands neighbour love, says just before it, “you shall reason frankly with your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:17).

Loving a neighbour never means staying in danger or enabling harm. If someone is abusing you, love for God, and even love for the one who is hurting you, does not require you to stay within reach. Safety comes first: get to a safe place, tell someone you trust, and report crimes to the police. The studies Getting On with People and Dealing with Difficult People give practical wisdom on love with limits.

Love your enemies

Jesus takes neighbour love to its furthest point. “But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:44–45). It is the family likeness of God, who loved us when we were his enemies. It may mean praying for them by name, refusing to repay insult with insult, and longing for their good, including their salvation. It does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong.

An example

A man finds his elderly next-door neighbour difficult. She complains about his children, his car and his bins. He does not like her. But when he notices she has not taken in her post for three days, he knocks, finds her unwell, and calls for help. Over the following weeks he takes her shopping. She is no less difficult. But he has begun to pray for her, and to his surprise he finds he would be sad if she moved away.

For reflection

Who is the neighbour you would rather pass by on the other side? How do the words “as yourself” search you? Is there someone you do not like whom you could love this week in deed and in truth? Where does love call you to speak the truth, or to set a limit, rather than simply to be nice?

6.title: When Love Grows Cold
6.essay:
Almost every Christian has times when love for God feels thin or dead: prayer is dry, the Bible flat, worship routine. Sometimes this is a warning; sometimes it is simply weather. This final chapter looks at both, and at what to do in the moment and afterwards.

Lost first love

The risen Christ wrote to the church in Ephesus with real praise. “But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first” (Revelation 2:4–5).

This church was busy and sound, yet their love had drained away. Jesus warned that in the last days “the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). Love can cool as a room cools when the fire is neglected.

His remedy has three parts: remember, repent, do. Remember what he has done, repent of what has crowded him out, and return to the simple, early habits of seeking him.

Not all dryness is the same

Drifting. Sometimes we have let other things crowd God out: busyness, screens, a grudge, a secret sin we will not give up. The coolness is a symptom, and the cure is repentance and return.

Weariness of body and mind. When Elijah asked to die, God let him sleep, and an angel brought food: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). Spiritual dryness is often bound up with depression, burnout or illness. If the flatness has lasted for weeks, if you have lost interest in most things, or if your sleep and appetite have changed, please see a doctor as well as talking to your pastor. Medicine is no failure of faith. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone now: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or speak to someone you trust today. The studies Depression & the Christian and Busy, Tired & Restless may help.

A season of God’s seeming distance. Sometimes, for reasons he does not explain, God withdraws the sense of his nearness, as the psalmists knew. The study Doubt & Faith speaks to times when God seems silent.

How love is renewed

We cannot generate love for God, but God gives and renews it. “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Love heads the list of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). So the first step is to ask. Paul prayed, “May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ” (2 Thessalonians 3:5). You can pray that for yourself.

God renews love by the ordinary means he has given: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of his people. They are where Christ has promised to meet us. Jude tells believers, “keep yourselves in the love of God” (Jude 21). We keep ourselves where his love shines, as someone cold sits in the sun. The study Spiritual Disciplines says more about these means of grace.

When your love is weak

Your safety does not rest on the strength of your love for God. It rests on his love for you. Paul writes: “For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

Think again of Peter. On the night of his denial his love failed completely. But Jesus had told him beforehand, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Christ’s love held Peter when Peter could not hold on. A cold Christian is not cast off, but called back. “A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3).

The fact that you are troubled by the coldness of your love is itself a sign of life. Dead hearts do not grieve over their deadness.

In the moment

When you sit down to pray and feel nothing, do not give up, and do not pretend. Tell God the truth: Lord, my heart is cold; I want to want you. That is a real prayer, and he hears it. Pray Psalm 63 or Psalm 73:25–26 as your own, even if the words feel bigger than you. Turn your attention from the temperature of your heart to the faithfulness of his.

When you face a person you do not feel like loving, ask one question: what would do this person good, right now? Then do it, asking God for help. Love often looks like nothing more than a small, chosen act of kindness.

Afterwards

Over time, ask what has been crowding God out. A sin you have stopped fighting, a grudge, a habit that fills every quiet moment? Confess it specifically, and receive his forgiveness: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Return to the first works: Scripture, prayer, Sunday worship, the Lord’s Table. Tell a trusted friend how you really are. Serve a neighbour: love for God is often rekindled in loving others. And be patient. Love grows the way trees grow, too slowly to watch, but surely.

An example

A church elder realises, during a busy year, that he has been leading Bible studies without opening his Bible for himself. He starts again, small: one psalm and one Gospel passage each morning, read slowly, with a short prayer. For weeks it feels mechanical. Then one morning, reading of Jesus washing the disciples’ feet, he finds himself in tears. Feelings come and go after that, but he no longer measures his love by them. He has remembered whose love holds him.

Loved to the end

We fall short of the great commandment every day. But Christ kept it for us and lives to make us like himself. One day we will love God and one another perfectly, for ever. Until then, begin where John began: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). And begin there again each day.

For reflection

Which kind of dryness best describes where you are now: drifting, weariness, or a season of God’s seeming distance? What might “remember, repent, do” mean for you this week? How does Romans 8:38–39 comfort you when your love is weak? Who could you tell honestly how your love for God is, and ask to pray with you?
